analytic.title: CACHING IN REAL-TIME RECONFIGURATION PORT SCHEDULING

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In reconfigurable systems, the concept of caching configu- rations can be employed to reduce the reconfiguration overhead, as already loaded configurations can be reused. In case reconfigurable systems are resources for real-time sys- tems, caching may even improve schedulability, as tasks can be executed immediately. The real-time reconfiguration port scheduling of this work combines mono processor schedul- ing algorithms and parallel slot execution, which particu- larly allows us to benefit from caching. However, a comprehensive design of methods is required. We discuss concepts for introducing caching to this new way of real-time scheduling on partially reconfigurable devices.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Reconfigurable devices combine flexibility and perfor- mance, bridging thereby the gap between ASICs and gen- eral purpose processors. Many applications that explore reconfigurable devices are located in the embedded sys- tems domain. There, the devices are part of reactive sys- tems that constantly interact with the environment. To re- spect these interactions, real-time capabilities the meeting of deadlines of tasks are required. When time sharing, i. e. run-time reconfiguration, becomes an issue, the long and sequential reconfiguration phases complicate real-time behavior. Partial reconfigurability reduces the overhead, as smaller area under reconfiguration also means shorter re- configuration time. Reconfiguration times are deterministic and reconfiguration phases are all dispatched by a single re- configuration port a mutually exclusive device similar to a uni-processor. The determinism and the similarity allows us to apply algorithms of the mono processor scheduling do- main, achieving a so-called reconfiguration port scheduling.

In order to further reduce the reconfiguration overhead, the reuse of already loaded configurations is applicable. Such a caching of configurations must be systematically introduced to reconfiguration port scheduling, as caching means the avoidance of reconfiguration phases, which are This work was partially funded by DFG SPP 1148. the core parameters of the port scheduling. In this work, we focus on the investigation of caching methods for periodic real-time task execution on reconfigurable architectures.

The paper is organized as follows. We summarize related work before we detail reconfiguration port scheduling and abstract the problem. In Sect. 4 and 5, we introduce offline and online caching methods. Section 6 discusses an example, before we conclude and give an outlook.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Caching for reconfigurable computing [1] is beneficial if applications to be executed are similar. If tasks are periodic, the reuse of already present stages improves a system. Con- figuration Caching [2] is also effective if the reconfigurable device is attached as a co-processor. [3] combines Configuration Prefetching and Configuration Caching, thereby dis- cussing the subject in some more detail. Besides these con- ceptual works, authors also investigate caching in coupled FPGA-processor systems [4]. History-based algorithm or specific constructs to denote stages worth to be cached are introduced. Real-time requirements are not considered.

In the area of scheduling tasks on partially reconfigurable FPGAs, the authors of [5] present an approach in the realm of our work. In their work, they optimize the area occupied, respecting the task time constraints, where tasks are not allowed to be preempted. In a similar approach, the authors of [6] analyze the effect of overall response time and guarantee-base scheduling when tasks comprise differ- ent shapes. If task preemption is allowed, the task acceptance rate is improved [7]. However, hardware task preemption represents additional costs due to still non-efficient techniques and methods available. Generally, we seldom find concepts that respect the reconfiguration time or the se- quentiality of the reconfiguration phases. Usually, both are neglected due to the assumption that the execution time is much higher than the reconfiguration time [7].

Finally, in [8], we find an approach that also considers real-time scheduling on partially reconfigurable FPGAs. In contrast to our approach, the scheduling is solved by algorithms of the parallel scheduling domain. When scheduling tasks onto reconfigurable fabrics, we face the problem of temporal area allocation. We have to provide enough computation space to serve the needs of arriv- ing tasks. If a set of real-time tasks is scheduled, sophisticated concepts are particularly needed.

We consider reconfigurable systems as multitasking units, as presented in e. g. [9,10]. Moreover, we apply a layered model to assign the temporal and spatial requirements each to a distinct layer, see Fig. 1. Basically, we organize the reconfigurable fabric of an FPGA into a slotted execu- tion environment such as the Erlangen Slot Machine [11]. The on top of the environment located scheduling layer assigns tasks to the slots of the environment. It accepts tasks not exceeding the maximum size of one slot. By this harmonization of the tasks, we avoid external fragmentation, i. e., the fragmentation of the fabric. Tasks that exceed the available size of a slot cannot be accepted.

div.head: Reconfiguration Port Scheduling
div.p: Our reconfiguration port scheduling is adopted from the real-time mono-processor scheduling domain. The reason for the adoption becomes obvious, when the characteristics of reconfigurable devices are considered in some more de- tail: The reconfiguration takes place sequentially via the mutually exclusive reconfiguration port. Mono-processor scheduling algorithms similarly dispatch tasks to a sequential and mutual exclusive processor. These algorithms are of low computation complexity and their adoption to reconfiguration port scheduling has proved to perform well [12].

We can compare the theory underlying our approach to the parallel machine problems with a single server [13]. The parallel machines of this approach are comparable to the re- configurable regions of our execution environment, while the server resembles the reconfiguration port. In contrast, we allow preempting the reconfiguration phase.

This preemption is realized by stopping the reconfiguration and resuming it at a later point in time. Such a be- havior, whose realizability also depends on the openness of the reconfiguration process, allows us to broaden the recon- figuration port scheduling, as preemption is a fundamental concept of many real-time scheduling algorithms. We do not preempt the execution phases of a task, as such a preemption could require a complete read-back of the current status of the computation area. As the reconfiguration of the same in- stance requires an additional reconfiguration phase, the time can add up to twice the original reconfiguration time. In contrast, preempted reconfigurations are resumed directly.

Nevertheless, the reconfiguration inevitably results in an overhead on modern FPGAs in the range of milliseconds. Thereby, the time is deterministic and proportional to the area under reconfiguration.

div.head: Problem Abstraction
div.p: Each task to be scheduled has an execution phase EX and a reconfiguration phase RT. While the former is the core of each instance of a task, the latter can be skipped if the correct configuration is already present in one of the slots.

Each task Ti has an execution (computation) time tEX,i and a period Ti. The deadline of the execution time is equal to the period, and can be computed for the kth instance by di,k= Ti k. The meeting of this deadlines is essential for a correct behavior of the system. In particular, the reconfiguration within each periodic instance of a task must finish early enough so that the task can meet its deadline. The lat- est finishing time for an RT phase can thus be calculated as d* = di-tEX,i. If the reconfiguration for a task can be re- alized before d*, the task will meet its overall deadline. We thus schedule the reconfiguration phases tRT,i with regard to their deadline d*. As the slots are of equal size, the time for the RT phase tRT,i is the same for all t.

We summarize our problem: We want to reduce the amount of reconfigurations when scheduling a task set F of n periodic tasks Ti onto an execution environment of m equally sized slots with m < n in general. Thereby, how- ever, caching means no RT phase. We have to bear in mind that by avoiding the RT phase, we undermine the concept of reconfiguration port scheduling, as the instance when the caching pays off, is an instance without tRT, i. e., tRT = 0

In general, caching improves schedulability and/or the maximum lateness. We are interested in which methods pro- vide the most promising solutions. Caching allows us to re- duce the maximum lateness of tasks or even increases the feasibility of task sets. Furthermore, we will also improve additional design goals like energy consumption, area con- sumption, resources needed, etc.
Our caching algorithms are based on the priority of the tasks, which we define on different characteristics of a task:

div.p: The first definition Pa is the same as in the classical mono-processor scheduling domain, where the calculation time ci of a task divided by the period Ti stands for the pri- ority. In contrast, Pb and Pc, along with Pa are defined for the purpose of static priority reconfiguration port schedul- ing, while Pd is suitable for dynamic priority assignment.

div.head: OFFLINE CACHING METHODS
div.p: We will introduce offline caching methods first, before considering on-line methods in Sec. 5. The algorithms apply static (fixed priority) as well as dynamic scheduling.

div.head: Priority Based Slot Reservation
div.p: If we can completely avoid the reconfiguration of a slot, we will have the maximum gain concerning the saved configurations, as only the initial configuration must be loaded. Our first concept presented the priority based slot reservation follows such a goal by statically analyzing the task set prior to the dispatching of the tasks to the slots. The applicability of the method depends on the number of slots available and on the characteristic of the task set. We prefer tasks with high priority, as those tasks get activated frequently. We reserve one or more slots exclusively for a corresponding amount of high priority tasks. The reserved slots are configured at set-up time and are from there on each exclusively used for their task only. The other tasks have to share the remaining slots. Figure 2 shows an example.

To select the tasks that exclusively occupy a slot, we can use either of the priorities Pa, Pb, or Pc, as all show good results. However, Pc particularly helps to indicate tasks that are worth to be cached. If the priority Pc is close to 1, this task would require nearly a slot on its own anyway, as the reconfiguration phase followed by the execution phase of this task would reside in a slot during the period of the task. Among the tasks having a high Pc, we prefer the tasks with a high Pb, as such a task will exploit the exclusively re- served slot longer than a task with a lower Pb. Furthermore, such a task would block one of the slots for the reconfiguration port scheduling for a disproportional long time.

To schedule the whole task set, we always require enough slots to be able to serve all tasks. In particular, if not all tasks are assigned to their exclusive slot (as is the case with m < n), there must always remain at least one slot that is not exclusively reserved for a task. Having only one slot left for reconfiguration inevitably means that hid- ing the reconfiguration latency cannot be applied any more. Therefore, we try to have at least two slots remaining.
In order to prove schedulability, we schedule the task set for the hyper period. The hyper period equals the least common multiplier of the task set.

Furthermore, concerning the set-up of the system, we have two possibilities to consider the configuration require-Fig. 3. Consecutive Task Combination with modification of the release times of tasks Ti and T2. ments of the fixed assigned tasks. Either, we denote the sum of the configuration times for these tasks as additional requirements that precedes the scheduling, or we include the configuration time into the calculation of the schedulability. The former eases to find a feasible schedule and will serve practical conditions in most cases, while the latter also allows us to consider systems without set-up time. However, the latter could extremely deform the system, if a large number of slots are exclusively reserved. In particular, as the reservation, i. e. the configuration, will only occur once.

If we consider the initial configuration of the exclusive slots within our feasibility analysis, we apply the earliest due date algorithm [14], as we first have to schedule a set of aperiodic tasks that have simultaneous arrival time. We then use a periodic scheduling algorithm for the remaining tasks.

Concerning the feasibility analysis of the priority based slot reservation, we first guarantee that the initialization phase can be realized without missing deadlines. After that the remaining tasks are scheduled until the first hyper-period of the task set is reached. The hyper-period is easy to sched- ule, as only the free tasks require reconfiguration, thus re- ducing the occupancy of the reconfiguration port.

div.head: Consecutive Task Combination
div.p: The consecutive task combination bases on the manipulation of the characteristics of the task set. If we combine two in- stance of a task and execute the EX phase of the first instance as late as possible, we can avoid the RT phase for the next instance. The finishing time of the first instance thereby will be at the end of the task's period, see Fig. 3.

If we combine two instances of a task Ti, we have to ensure that no other task Tj will reconfigure the slot in the meantime. We adapt the release time of the first instance and the deadline of the second instance. The new release time r of task i and instance k can be calculated by ri,k k Ti-(tRT + tEX,i). Similar, the new absolute deadline d for the task i and instance k + 1 is di,k+1 = ri,+l + tEx,i Moreover, for instance k + 1, we do not have to consider the task Ti for the reconfiguration port scheduling, as it does not require an RT phase. Thus, the relevant deadline is the deadline d,; of the instance Ti,k.

Alternatively, we can allow the tasks some slack by releasing the task prior to the new release time r. Then, we have to block the slot after finishing the execution phase of instance k until the beginning of the instance k + 1. Such a modification can be accepted if the blocking time is smaller than the tRT, as due to the avoidance of the RT phase for the instance k + 1, a complete tRT is saved. In general, we can approach the problem by using a resource access protocol.

In Fig. 3 only some of the tasks are combined for consecutive task combination. This partial modification makes particularly sense, if more tasks than slots available resem- ble a similar period. Modifying all such tasks would mean that they would each occupy a slot at the similar time.

The advantage of the approach is the reduction of the re- configuration phases required by two for those tasks whose instances are combined. Tasks with short periods may be preferred, as their overall fraction of the reconfiguration time is larger than of those tasks with longer periods. The approach can improve the scheduling of tasks when for the priority Pc holds PC < 1 without permanently reserving slots for specific tasks as in the preceding approach.

div.head: DYNAMIC / ON-LINE
div.p: While the first two algorithms manipulated the task set of- fline, the remaining ones will focus on online conditions.

div.head: Scheduling Look Back
div.p: The first approach, scheduling look back (SLB), considers the condition of the slots before starting an instance of an RT phase. If any of the slots already holds the configuration of the newly arriving task, the RT phase is omitted in favor of immediately starting the EX phase. Figure 4 depicts an example, where the second reconfiguration of the frequently occurring task Ti can be avoided.

Additionally to tasks with short periods, we improve the schedulability of tasks that are started relatively late, as their next invocation is close to the finishing time. Despite that the next release of the task will be soon, the reconfiguration of the task is often postponed, as the priority is too low. Here, we can temporarily inherit the priority of a higher priority task. Such a behavior can be controlled by a resource access protocol. Those protocols allow low priority tasks to inherit priorities by still ensuring feasibility of a task set. Moreover, we do not have to pre-compute the task set. If we have a task set that is feasible without SLB, the perfor- mance of the task set will be improved by applying SLB.

div.head: Scheduling Look Ahead
div.p: A different approach is scheduling look ahead (SLA). As implied by the name, it looks into the future, opposed to SLB, which only refers to the current status and former al- location of the slots. SLA becomes active each time the reconfiguration port idles. If we can already start a reconfiguration phase of a task that is released in the future, and do not harm the other tasks, the performance of the algorithm can be improved. Figure 5 depicts an example.

SLB relies on several characteristics of the task set. As we know the whole task set from the beginning of the scheduling, we particularly know when a new instance of a task is released. Thus, as the EX phase of a task can start at the beginning of the period, we can start with the RT phase before the final release of the task.

The pre-loading can only take place if (1) the reconfiguration port is free and (2) the time until the release time of the instance of the task selected is less or equal the reconfiguration time of this tasks. Otherwise, we might reconfigure a task Ti, mark it as already reconfigured (so that it can be executed immediately when the next instance is released), and another task Tj uses this slot for reconfiguration before we have executed task Ti.

div.p: We have set up a simulator to evaluate the algorithms. Non- feasible tasks can be found task sets can be rated by performing the scheduling algorithms on a set of task sets. Figure 6 c) displays the latter sce- nario, where the scheduling is still improved comparing to the scheduling without configuration caching.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In this work, we have presented caching concepts for reconfiguration port scheduling. Caching, in general, is driven by the overall design goal that reconfiguration should be avoided as often as possible. When scheduling the recon- figuration phases, we therefore improve the performance of real-time scheduling of tasks on reconfigurable devices. The four methods presented are two offline and two on-line al- gorithms. We plan to include the results of this work into a system that heuristically searches feasible schedules even if the reconfiguration port occupancy is larger than 1, where schedulability would be impossible without caching.
